title: Symptoms of a penalty that is too weak
text: A large share of samples violates a specific constraint, and the best samples by energy are infeasible. Raise that constraint's weight (x1.5 to x2 per round is a common step). Change one constraint at a time when several are violated, starting with the most violated.
source: standard practice; Glover et al. QUBO tutorial 2019

title: Symptoms of a penalty that is too strong
text: Feasibility is near 100% but the best feasible objective is far from the reference and samples cluster on a few mediocre feasible states. The penalty dominates the landscape, so objective differences become small relative to the annealing temperature or the hardware's coefficient resolution. Lower the weight toward (never below) the penalty lower bound; it often helps more than extra sampling.
source: standard practice; Lucas 2014 discussion of penalty magnitudes

title: Penalty lower bound
text: With integer penalties whose smallest violation is 1, a weight larger than the largest objective gain from flipping one variable stops single flips from making an infeasible state better. It is a heuristic floor, not a proof for multi-variable moves; the loop refuses weights below it. Good weights are usually 1x to a few x this floor.

title: Insufficient sampling
text: Feasibility is fine and penalties look balanced, but the gap stays positive and results vary between rounds with the same config. Increase effort: num_sweeps / num_reads (SA), num_reads or annealing_time (D-Wave), time_limit_sec (Fujitsu). Prefer changing one effort parameter at a time so its effect is visible.

title: Do not compare energies across rounds
text: Changing penalty weights or scale changes the energy landscape, so QUBO energies from different rounds are not comparable. Judge improvement only on the original objective, feasibility and gap; use energy only to diagnose within a round.

title: Chain breaks on D-Wave
text: If the chain-break fraction is high (rule of thumb: more than a few percent of samples), raise chain_strength moderately; if chains never break but quality is poor, chain_strength may be too large and compress the problem's couplings, so try lowering it. Long chains (dense problems) make both effects worse. See tk-chain-measured: on a dense 30-variable problem the default produced breaks in 99% of samples.

title: Precision loss from large coefficient ranges
text: When the ratio between the largest and smallest QUBO coefficients is large (typical for squared slack penalties), hardware with limited coefficient resolution or auto-scaling loses the small objective terms. Remedies: use the smallest safe penalty weight, rescale, or (as a formulation rewrite) avoid slack encodings. Uniform scaling alone does not change the ratio.
source: standard practice; D-Wave h/J range documentation

title: When to stop
text: Stop when the gap reaches the target, when several rounds bring no improvement in best feasible objective, or when effort parameters are at their caps and penalties are balanced (low violations, objective not improving). Re-running the same configuration wastes budget.

title: Measured: chain strength on a dense 30-variable QUBO (D-Wave)
text: select_k n=30 k=6 (cardinality penalty couples all 435 pairs; ~120-134 qubits, max chain 5-6) on Advantage_system4, 100 reads each, one run per setting. Default uniform-torque chain_strength 86: 17% of chains broken, 99% of samples had a break, feasibility 1%, best 81/110. 0.25x and 0.5x: 54-74% broken, 0% feasible. 2x: breaks ~0%, feasibility 4%. 4x: no breaks, feasibility 4%, best 90/110. SA on the same QUBO: 97% feasible, optimum found. Lessons: on dense penalty QUBOs the default chain strength can be far too weak (check samples_with_chain_breaks, not only the mean fraction); removing breaks is necessary but not sufficient, because a large chain_strength compresses the problem's couplings in the auto-scaled range (precision_loss), so penalty weights and chain strength must be tuned together.
source: our experiment scripts/exp_dwave_chain_strength.py, 2026-10-04 (single run per setting)

title: Chain strength: what benchmark studies report
text: Benchmark studies across D-Wave generations find an optimal chain strength that depends on problem density and hardware, typically a small multiple (about 1-2x) of the largest problem coupling |J| after scaling; larger values reduce chain breaks but lower solution quality. Scanning several embeddings and chain strengths, and tuning annealing time, is recommended. An open-source optimizer exists (github.com/HunpyoLee/OptimizeChainStrength).
source: Pelofske, Comparing three generations of D-Wave quantum annealers (Quantum Sci. Technol. 2025, arXiv:2301.03009); Benchmarking Chain Strength (NSF PAR 10477832)

title: Annealing time and time-to-solution
text: Time-to-solution should be optimised over annealing time; for dense problems (SK, dense Max-Cut) success probability falls roughly like exp(-(N/N0)^2) at fixed schedule, and newer hardware (Advantage2) sampled optima reliably at long (1 ms) anneals where older devices did not. Longer anneals are not always better within a fixed budget: combine with fewer reads.

title: Published methods for choosing penalty weights
text: Exact upper bounds that guarantee the QUBO optimum is feasible: sum of absolute objective coefficients (loosest), posiform/negaform bounds, and Verma-Lewis (largest objective gain from any single flip that violates a constraint; usually closest to the best weights). Too-large exact bounds hurt annealers, so sequential/adaptive schemes start low and raise weights while infeasible samples appear (studied on a Digital Annealer), and ML models have been trained to predict good penalty multipliers from instance features. Our penalty_lower_bound is the Verma-Lewis single-flip quantity used as a floor.
source: Verma & Lewis, Discrete Optimization 2020 (Penalty and partitioning techniques...); Ayodele et al., GECCO 2022 (Exact and sequential penalty weights... with a digital annealer); Minimum Bisection ML penalty tuning (arXiv:2509.19005)

title: Measured on SA: slack vs. unbalanced encoding for a capacity inequality
text: Random 0/1 knapsack, n = 40 and 60 items (values 1-30, weights 1-20, capacity 40% of total weight), SA defaults (100 reads x 1000 sweeps), 5 seeds, training instances only. Binary slack with weight just above the floor (31): mean gap 20-27%. Binary slack with a large weight (1000): 26-31%, worse, because the squared slack penalty dominates the landscape. Unbalanced penalization with weight 1, l1 about one third of the largest objective coefficient (l1 = 10 for values up to 30) and l2 = 0.25-1: mean gap 2-7%, 100% feasible, no slack variables. Too large an l1 (40 with l2 = 0.25) gave 15-29%. Implication: for capacity-type inequalities on SA, try unbalanced first; exactness of slack encodings does not translate into better solutions.
source: our SA experiment on training instances (seeds 1000-1001), 2026-10-04
